strengths: The Open Proof Corpus addresses a genuine and important gap: there is a severe shortage of large-scale, human-verified LLM-generated proofs, and this paper provides 5,000+ proofs across 1,000+ problems graded by qualified judges (former IMO participants), which is a substantial resource for the community.

The dataset creation methodology is unusually careful and transparent: pilot phase, detailed grading guidelines, abstention/uncertainty mechanisms, ~10% double-grading with an estimated judge error rate (p=5%), coordinator monitoring, and an explicit bias check when LLM issue summaries were introduced to the grading pipeline.

The paper goes beyond dataset release to answer several substantiated open questions: quantifying the formal-vs-informal proof gap on a common problem set (PutnamBench), showing final-answer accuracy is a poor proxy for proof validity (with per-model variation, e.g., o3 dropping ~28 points), and demonstrating pairwise ranking methods substantially outperform pointwise best-of-n selection.

The demonstration of utility is concrete: GRPO fine-tuning of an 8B model on the OPC achieves 88.1% judgment accuracy, matching GEMINI-2.5-PRO's majority-vote performance, with a reasonably sized held-out test set (293 proofs) and strong baselines including cost reporting.

Good positioning against concurrent and prior work (Petrov et al., Mahdavi et al., Guo et al., Sheng et al.), with clear articulation of what distinguishes the OPC (scale, open sourcing, correct/incorrect proof balance, compatibility with established benchmarks).
Reproducibility is supported by released prompts (App. E), grading instructions, competition breakdown with difficulty proxies (Table 4), and the open-sourced fine-tuned model.
weaknesses: Label quality is fundamentally binary and somewhat noisy: only ~10% double-graded, a 5% estimated judge error rate is non-trivial for fine-grained proof correctness, and the 90.4% 'human baseline' is measured on the double-graded subset rather than a dedicated adjudicated test set.

The best-of-n analysis is weakly powered and slightly inconsistent: the pass@n vs. selection-method comparison (Fig. 6) uses only 60 problems, and the headline numbers in the introduction (26%→36%, 47% for ranking) do not match the full-subset results in Fig. 7 (22.7%→31.4%, 40%), which is confusing; Rank (Bracket) is also dropped from the full-subset evaluation without a clear justification.

The fine-tuned judge model (OPC-R1-8B) is evaluated in-distribution on a test split drawn from the same generic subset, which the authors acknowledge; there is no out-of-distribution evaluation (e.g., on MathArena or PutnamBench proofs), so the claimed parity with GEMINI-2.5-PRO may overstate generalization.

Several hyperlinks and interface URLs are missing/blank in the manuscript (§3.2 grading interface, judge guidelines in App. D), which undermines the reproducibility claims for the grading pipeline as presented.

Contamination is a real concern given the public competition sources, and the mitigation ('the main purpose is not benchmarking') is somewhat hand-wavy, especially since §5.1 and §5.4 do present model comparisons on these problems.

Only six models contribute proofs, with skewed distribution (O4-MINI 1,615 vs. DeepSeek-R1 326), and the corpus is limited to high-school-level competitions; the paper itself notes the lack of undergraduate/research-level coverage.

The self-judging analysis (Table 3) is interesting but based on a small judge×prover grid and lacks error bars or significance testing throughout the paper, making several of the claimed gaps (e.g., 3% Swiss vs. Bracket margin) hard to assess statistically.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: there are very few large-scale, human-evaluated datasets of LLM-generated mathematical proofs, and the OPC (5,062 proofs across 1,010 problems) is substantially larger and more open than prior efforts (Petrov et al., Mahdavi et al., Guo et al.).

The dataset construction methodology is unusually careful for this kind of resource: 13 qualified judges (former IMO participants/olympiad finalists), a pilot phase, an iterative grading interface, abstention/uncertainty flags, and ~10% double-grading with an explicit inter-annotator agreement analysis (90.4% agreement, estimated per-judge error rate of ~5%).

The paper uses the dataset to answer concrete, previously unresolved empirical questions rather than only releasing data: the formal vs. natural language gap (11x on PutnamBench), the final-answer vs. proof-validity gap (up to ~30% drop for o3), and a systematic best-of-n comparison including pairwise ranking strategies, which yields actionable findings (ranking methods scale past n=5 where discrete/continuous selection plateaus).

The fine-tuning experiment (GRPO on DEEPSEEK-R1-QWEN3-8B) provides a concrete demonstration of downstream utility: the 8B model matches GEMINI-2.5-PRO at 88.1% judgment accuracy, a 17-point improvement over its base model.
Qualitative error taxonomy in App. C (inequality sign reversals, geometry angle failures, overgeneralization, pathological citation behavior) is a useful contribution for the community.
The paper is largely transparent about limitations (contamination risk, high-school-level focus, distribution-matched train/test for the fine-tuned judge).
weaknesses: Label reliability is thinner than the headline claims suggest: only ~10% of proofs are double-graded, agreement is used as a proxy for human accuracy (agreement between two fallible judges is not the same as correctness), and most proofs receive a single binary judgment. The binary correct/incorrect label also discards substantial information (severity of errors, partial credit) that the 0-7 scoring used elsewhere could have provided.

A potential circularity/bias concern: LLM-generated issue summaries (O4-MINI) were shown to human judges for a large fraction of the dataset, which could anchor judge decisions toward the model's identified issues. The before/after agreement-rate check is indirect and does not rule out systematic drift in which errors are caught (e.g., the summaries list at most four issues).

The fine-tuned judge (OPC-R1-8B) is trained and tested on splits from the same generic subset with the same distribution; the paper itself acknowledges OOD degradation. Claims of matching GEMINI-2.5-PRO therefore overstate the result, since the closed model's performance was not obtained with in-distribution training. Evaluation on the MathArena or PutnamBench subsets would have substantially strengthened this claim.

Several reproducibility gaps in the manuscript itself: multiple URLs are literally blank in the text (grading interface 'available at [blank]', full guidelines reference on p.4 and p.18), which undermines the 'fully open-sourced' positioning relative to prior work. Table 1 uses 'GEMINI-PRO' inconsistently vs. GEMINI-2.5-PRO elsewhere.

Coverage limitations are significant: nearly all problems are high-school competition level, so conclusions about proof generation may not transfer to research-level mathematics; contamination from publicly available competition problems is acknowledged but not measured (no membership-inference or decontamination analysis).

Some analyses are underpowered: the best-of-n comparison with full human judgments on all 8 generations covers only 60 problems, and Rank (Bracket) was never evaluated on the full subset, making the headline '47%' and the Swiss-vs-Bracket 3% margin less robust than presented.

The best-of-n results are tied to a single prover (O4-MINI) and a single judge (O4-MINI); it is unclear whether the ranking-based selection gains generalize across provers or judges, particularly given the demonstrated self-judging bias in Table 3.

Novelty of the analysis contributions is moderate: the final-answer vs. proof gap was already reported by concurrent work (Guo et al., 2025b), and the self-preference finding confirms known results (Panickssery et al., 2024); the dataset itself is the main contribution, so its long-term impact depends on adoption, which cannot be assessed yet.

strengths: Significant and timely resource contribution: the Open Proof Corpus (5,062 human-evaluated proofs across 1,010 competition problems) addresses a real gap, as prior proof-evaluation efforts are small, use outdated models, or are not open-sourced.

Rigorous and transparent data collection methodology: 13 judges recruited from former IMO participants/selection finalists, a pilot phase, clear grading guidelines, a custom grading interface, ~10% double-grading with an explicit noise estimate (individual judge error rate p = 5%), and coordinator-based discrepancy resolution.

The dataset design directly supports the posed research questions (PutnamBench subset for formal vs. informal comparison, MathArena subset for final-answer vs. proof-validity analysis, best-of-n subset with 8 generations per problem), and the paper answers these questions with concrete, quantified findings (e.g., 11x gap for informal vs. formal; 30% drop for o3 between final-answer and proof correctness; ranking-based best-of-n reaching 47%).

Useful downstream demonstration: GRPO fine-tuning of an 8B model on the OPC reaches 88.1% judgment accuracy, matching Gemini-2.5-Pro's majority-vote performance and improving 17% over its base model, evidencing the dataset's training value.

Interesting empirical findings beyond the headline claims, e.g., models rarely admit inability to solve problems, and LLM judges perform significantly worse on their own proofs (Table 3), with reasonable engagement of prior conflicting results (Petrov et al.).
Complete prompts, grading instructions, and qualitative error analyses are provided in the appendices, supporting reproducibility and reuse.
weaknesses: Label granularity is limited: proofs are binary correct/incorrect, with the correctness threshold ('correct even if it would earn 5+/7') somewhat arbitrary; borderline judgments (which dominate subtle-error cases) may be noisy, and uncertain/abstained judgments (<3%) plus single-judge labels for ~90% of data leave residual noise unquantified per-sample.

The headline fine-tuned model result (OPC-R1-8B) is evaluated on a test set drawn from the same distribution as training data, which the authors themselves acknowledge; no out-of-distribution evaluation is provided, weakening the claim of 'on-par with Gemini-2.5-Pro'.

The formal vs. informal comparison (§5.3) is somewhat apples-to-oranges: DeepSeek-Prover-V2 is a specialized Lean model evaluated on PutnamBench while general-purpose models are given informal prompts (and even the informal final answer appended for Putnam problems), so the '11x' gap conclusion conflates model specialization, benchmark adaptation, and evaluation protocol differences.

Several data sources are marked 'Private' (e.g., Romanian Masters, SMT 2025) and multiple URLs in App. D are blank/incomplete ('can be accessed online at  and'), creating reproducibility gaps and potential licensing/redistribution concerns for competition material.
Data contamination risk is acknowledged (public competition problems likely in training corpora) but only superficially mitigated; this undermines some of the benchmarking-style conclusions in §5.1.

The scientific novelty beyond the dataset is moderate: the best-of-n ranking experiments largely adapt Liu et al. (2025), and the main analyses are descriptive statistics rather than new methods; the judge-bias finding (Table 3) is based on a small subset of judge-prover combinations.

Double-grading coverage (10%) and the independence assumption underlying the p = 5% error-rate estimate (judges may correlate, and most 'agreements' may be on clearly incorrect proofs) make the label-noise analysis optimistic.

strengths: Significant community resource: the OPC is the first large-scale, open-sourced, human-validated dataset of LLM-generated proofs (5,062 proofs, 1,010 competition problems, six SOTA models), addressing a clear gap since prior proof-evaluation efforts are small, closed, or use outdated models.

Careful and transparent annotation methodology: 13 expert judges (former IMO participants/selection finalists), custom grading interface, well-documented grading guidelines, pilot phase with ~35% double-grading, ~10% double-grading overall with 90.4% inter-judge agreement and an estimated 5% individual error rate, abstention/uncertainty flags, and a bias check for the LLM issue-summary feature.

The dataset is used to answer substantive open questions rather than being released in isolation: (1) quantified formal vs. informal proof gap (Gemini-2.5-Pro ~4x Goedel-Prover-V2 on PutnamBench), (2) demonstrated divergence between final-answer accuracy and proof correctness (e.g., o3 drops ~30%), (3) systematic evaluation of best-of-n selection strategies including novel Swiss/Bradley-Terry ranking (26% -> 47%), and (4) a self-evaluation bias analysis.

Demonstrated downstream utility: GRPO fine-tuning of an 8B model reaches 83.8% pass@1 / 88.1% maj@5 judging accuracy, matching Gemini-2.5-Pro and approaching GPT-5, with a genuine OOD evaluation on undergraduate-level problems showing the improvement persists out of distribution.

Thorough robustness work: contamination analysis (standard vs. non-standard competition split; worst-case ground-truth-provided experiment), honest discussion of the in-distribution train/test overlap for OPC-R1-8B, confidence intervals throughout, and detailed prompts, interface screenshots, and training hyperparameters in appendices enabling reproduction.

Honest and well-scoped limitations section (models released after data collection, high-school-level focus) and qualitative failure-mode analysis (inequality sign errors, geometry struggles, overgeneralization, odd Gemini citation behavior) that adds practical value.
weaknesses: Key best-of-n results rest on a small base: the pass@n comparison uses only 60 problems with full human judgments, and even the larger subset has 134 problems with relatively large confidence intervals; Rank (Bracket) is not evaluated on the full subset, weakening the comparison between ranking methods.

Problem selection was adaptively adjusted during annotation based on ongoing model performance and the conclusions the authors aimed to draw, which introduces some risk of distribution bias and makes the corpus composition partially outcome-dependent (acknowledged only implicitly).

The 'LLMs are human-level judges' claim relies on a human baseline (90.4%) measured on all double-graded proofs rather than the test subset, and the fine-tuned model's headline result is partly in-distribution; while OOD checks mitigate this, the headline framing is slightly stronger than the evidence.

Binary correct/incorrect labels discard severity information; the continuous-score capability is explored only within the best-of-n experiment, and finer-grained human grades (e.g., the 0-7 scale the guidelines reference) would have increased the dataset's research value.

Several findings (final-answer vs. proof gap) largely confirm prior work (Guo et al., 2025b; Mahdavi et al., 2025), with the main novelty being scale, openness, and established-benchmark grounding rather than fundamentally new scientific insight.

Contamination cannot be fully ruled out for the public competition problems, and the authors concede the Gemini-2.5-Pro vs. o4-mini comparison in 5.1 may be affected; the 2% SMT 2025 problems are withheld, creating a small incompleteness in the released resource.

strengths: The core resource is genuinely useful: >5,000 human-evaluated LLM-generated proofs over 1,000 competition problems, graded by 13 expert judges (former IMO participants), which the related-work section convincingly shows is a gap relative to prior proof-evaluation efforts (Petrov et al., 2025; Mahdavi et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025b).

The annotation methodology is unusually well documented for a dataset paper: grading guidelines, abstention/uncertainty flags, ~10% double-grading with an inter-judge agreement estimate (90.4%, error rate p≈5%), a pilot phase, and released interface/guidelines/prompts in the appendix.

The paper addresses concrete, previously open empirical questions: (1) the informal-vs-formal proof gap on PutnamBench, (2) the divergence between final-answer accuracy and proof correctness on MathArena, and (3) best-of-n selection strategies, where pairwise ranking methods (Swiss/Bracket with Bradley-Terry) are a sensible and somewhat novel application.

Reasonable due diligence on confounds: a worst-case experiment giving judges the ground-truth solution (Table 4), a contamination analysis contrasting 'standard' vs 'non-standard' competitions (Fig. 8), and an out-of-distribution evaluation of the fine-tuned model on Putnam problems (Table 6).

Transparency about problems: the authors disclose a bug in the Rank (Swiss) method, the in-distribution concern for OPC-R1-8B, and the withheld SMT 2025 problems, with code and data provided for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Problem selection was adaptively steered during annotation ('problem prioritization was adjusted based on ongoing performance metrics... and progress towards the specific conclusions we aimed to draw from the dataset'). This circularity between data curation and intended conclusions undermines the claim that the dataset neutrally 'resolves open questions'; the headline statistics (e.g., the ~50% target accuracy, the partition discrepancies in Fig. 3) are partly artifacts of this curation process.

The flagship fine-tuning result is overstated. OPC-R1-8B's 88.1% is achieved on a test set drawn from the same distribution as its training data; on the out-of-distribution undergraduate subset it drops to 75.0, well below O4-MINI (83.8) and GPT-5 (83.6). The abstract's claim of 'matching GEMINI-2.5-PRO and performing close to GPT-5' does not survive this OOD test, and the fine-tuned model's value proposition is weaker than presented.

The claim that GPT-5 judging is 'on-par with human performance' is not supported: human agreement is 90.4±3.4 and GPT-5 pass@1 is 89.3±3.5 — overlapping CIs mean statistical indistinguishability, not parity, and 'human performance' here is measured as agreement between two fallible judges (each with ~5% error), not ground truth.

Key quantitative conclusions rest on small subsets: the pass@n comparison in Fig. 6(a) uses only 60 problems, the full best-of-n subset has 134 problems with large confidence intervals (acknowledged), and Rank (Bracket) was never evaluated on the larger subset. Given that Fig. 6(b) presents Swiss vs discrete differences (~7%) with wide CIs, the significance of the ranking-method superiority is not established.

Contamination risk is mitigated but not resolved: most problems are from publicly available competitions (IMO Shortlist, USAMO, etc.), and the contamination analysis (Fig. 8) compares performance across competition classes, which conflates contamination with difficulty — the authors themselves admit this 'cannot definitively discount' contamination. For a dataset intended as a benchmark, public sourcing is a durability concern.

Labels are purely binary ('correct/incorrect') despite the grading philosophy being explicitly rubric-based (5+/7 points); the discarded severity information limits downstream use (e.g., as reward signal for proof generation training) relative to what the annotation effort could have supported.

Some analyses are thin: Table 3's self-evaluation breakdown covers only four prover models on an unspecified subset; the 'uncertainty acknowledgment' finding (114 instances out of 1,700) is anecdotal; and the MathArena subset retains only proofs with correct final answers, biasing the conditional proof-correctness analysis in §5.4.

strengths: Significant and timely resource contribution: the OPC is the first large-scale (5,062 proofs, 1,010 problems), openly released dataset of human-evaluated LLM-generated proofs on prestigious competition problems, addressing a clear gap identified in prior small-scale or closed evaluations.

Impressively rigorous annotation methodology: 13 expert judges (former IMO participants), detailed grading guidelines, a pilot phase, ~10% double-grading with quantified inter-judge agreement (90.4%, estimated judge error rate p=5%), abstention/uncertainty flags, and a careful bias analysis for the LLM issue-summary feature.

The dataset enables multiple substantive empirical findings rather than being a bare resource: (1) natural-language proofs substantially outperform formal provers on PutnamBench, (2) a measurable and model-dependent gap between final-answer accuracy and proof correctness, (3) pairwise-ranking best-of-n selection clearly beats discrete/continuous self-verification, (4) self-evaluation bias (models judge their own proofs worse), and (5) strong LLM judging performance approaching human level.

Strong downstream demonstration: fine-tuning R1-Qwen3-8B with GRPO on the OPC yields 88.1% judgment accuracy, competitive with frontier models, with an OOD evaluation on undergraduate-level problems and a proper train/test split by problem.

Thorough treatment of threats to validity: contamination analysis (standard vs. non-standard competitions, worst-case ground-truth-solution experiment), 95% confidence intervals throughout, and a candid limitations section (e.g., acknowledged in-distribution test set for OPC-R1-8B, exclusion of GPT-5/Grok-4 as provers).

Good reproducibility practices: dataset and code in supplementary material, full prompts in the appendix, transparent reporting of anomalies (e.g., the Rank (Swiss) bug affecting 18 questions, Gemini's spurious IMOSL 2004 G8 citations).
weaknesses: The informal-vs-formal comparison in §5.3 is somewhat confounded: Gemini-2.5-Pro (a general-purpose frontier model) is compared against specialized formal provers (Goedel-Prover-V2), which differ in scale, training data, and adaptation; the paper acknowledges Seed-Prover's 50% accuracy but the headline '4x more problems' claim invites an apples-to-oranges interpretation.

Some headline analyses rest on small samples: the pass@n vs. best-of-n comparison uses only 60 fully-judged problems, and the best-of-n subset is 134 problems with correspondingly wide confidence intervals; Rank (Bracket) was not evaluated on the full subset.

Binary correct/incorrect labels discard grading nuance; a 5% estimated individual judge error rate is non-trivial, and the independence assumption underlying the (1-p)^2 + p^2 estimate may not hold (correlated judgments could hide larger correlated error).

Problem selection was dynamically adapted during annotation based on observed model performance to steer toward targeted conclusions, which introduces a degree of experimenter degrees of freedom and makes the dataset composition partly outcome-dependent.

Judge grading criteria are inherently somewhat subjective (e.g., 'trivial step', 'well-known theorem with a Wikipedia page'); while documented, sensitivity of the main conclusions to these thresholds is not analyzed.

Coverage is limited to competition-style mathematics (84% high-school level) and pre-GPT-5/Grok-4 provers, so conclusions about proof-generation capability may not extrapolate to research-level mathematics or the newest models.
